questions.prompt: Why does resetting the krbtgt password only once fail to invalidate an existing Golden Ticket?
options: Because the reset takes 30 days to take effect
Because Active Directory retains both the current and previous krbtgt hash, so a ticket signed with the old hash still decrypts successfully
Because Golden Tickets are stored on domain controllers permanently
It does invalidate it; a second reset is purely optional hygiene
questions.explanation: AD keeps two krbtgt hashes for backward compatibility. A single reset makes the compromised hash the 'previous' one, which DCs still accept -- only the second reset flushes it out entirely.

questions.prompt: Why is the recommended wait between the two krbtgt resets 10 hours specifically?
options: It is an arbitrary number chosen for convenience
It corresponds to the default Maximum lifetime for user ticket and service ticket policy settings, and allows all DCs to replicate the change
Because Kerberos requires exactly 10 hours to regenerate keys
Because domain controllers only replicate once per 10 hours
questions.explanation: The 10-hour figure tracks the default Kerberos ticket lifetime settings and gives replication time to converge. Where those lifetime policies have been changed, the wait should exceed the configured value.

questions.prompt: What is the tradeoff of resetting krbtgt twice in rapid succession rather than waiting?
options: There is no tradeoff; rapid succession is always preferred

It invalidates all existing TGTs immediately, forcing every client to re-authenticate and likely requiring application service restarts -- disruptive, but sometimes warranted by a confirmed compromise
It permanently corrupts the krbtgt account
It only works on domains with a single domain controller
questions.explanation: Rapid succession is the emergency breach-recovery path: it kills forged tickets immediately at the cost of domain-wide authentication disruption. The staged approach is safer but leaves forged tickets valid longer.

questions.prompt: Why should domain controller replication health be verified before the first reset?
options: Because replication health has no bearing on the reset
Because a reset that doesn't replicate cleanly leaves some DCs holding the new key and others the old one, causing intermittent authentication failures on top of an active incident
Because replication must be manually disabled first
Because the reset script requires an offline domain
questions.explanation: Partial replication of a krbtgt change produces inconsistent key state across DCs, which manifests as intermittent, hard-to-diagnose authentication failures -- especially damaging mid-incident.
